extracted.intended_audience: college/university mathematics instructors and communication educators (those assessing or teaching mathematical writing and presentations)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and resources for designing, scoring, and giving feedback on student mathematical writing and presentations (undergraduate/graduate), including rubrics, criteria, and assessment practices. Emphasizes both pedagogical techniques and concrete dimensions of quality in math communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying and prioritizing assessment criteria before grading
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifying and prioritizing assessment criteria before grading is important to prevent unintentional, subconscious bias, even in graders who consider themselves objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly choose and order rubrically-important criteria prior to looking at student work to reduce bias; see cited study (Uhlmann and Cohen) showing how post-hoc criteria selection can justify discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of effective student talks and papers
rubrics_metrics.description: A collection of characteristics that define effective student mathematical talks and written papers (title used as umbrella for specific dimensions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See linked page 'Characteristics of Effective Communication' for concrete traits; this entry is an umbrella for more specific criteria such as audience awareness, structure, precision, and use of visuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: General principles of mathematical communication
rubrics_metrics.description: High-level principles that guide writing and speaking about mathematics for learning and for professional communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principles organize choices about focus, rigor, audience, and style; consult the site's sections on writing, presentations, and pedagogy for elaboration and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focusing and structuring longer communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that longer pieces (term papers, reports, long talks) have an appropriate focus and clear internal structure so that they remain coherent across many pages or minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes choosing an appropriate scope, breaking content into sections, and using signposting; see 'Focusing and structuring longer communication' resources for templates and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding the audience through the content
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly lead readers/listeners through arguments and results so they can follow the flow of ideas and see how parts connect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use introductions, roadmaps, transitions, summaries, and reminders of goals to orient the audience; consider both conceptual signposting and formal markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering information so content flows logically
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange definitions, lemmas, proofs, examples, and motivations in an order that produces a logical and comprehensible narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize the order that best aids comprehension (motivation before formalism when appropriate), and avoid jarring reordering that forces the audience to backtrack frequently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive connectivity: too much of a good thing
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware of over-linking or over-signposting that can overwhelm or distract the audience instead of clarifying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance connectivity: provide enough signposts to guide without creating fragmentation; examples and anti-patterns discussed on the site.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing conceptual with formal
rubrics_metrics.description: Strike an appropriate balance between conceptual explanation (intuition, examples) and formal statements/proofs depending on audience and purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For learning-focused pieces emphasize intuition and examples; for research or formal expositions emphasize precision and formalism while still motivating results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure statements, definitions, and proofs are precise and satisfy standards of mathematical rigor appropriate to the audience and venue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether claims are stated clearly, hypotheses are explicit, and proofs justify assertions; consider whether the level of rigor matches course/discipline expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of proof & proof-writing strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and use appropriate proof types (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, induction, etc.) and strategies tailored to the problem and audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should note whether chosen proof strategies are appropriate, clearly explained, and whether alternative approaches would be preferred for clarity or pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof writing; guiding text
rubrics_metrics.description: Use surrounding explanatory text to guide readers through proofs rather than presenting a bare sequence of symbolic steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good proofs are accompanied by a short explanation of the approach, intermediate roadmaps within long proofs, and comments that indicate the purpose of technical lemmas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof elegance
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate proofs for elegance: conciseness, insightful steps, clever ideas, and avoidance of unnecessary technical baggage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elegance is context-dependent; prefer simpler, more illuminating arguments when they do not sacrifice necessary rigor or completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Write and speak with sensitivity to the intended audience's background, needs, and expectations (e.g., majors vs. non-majors, peers vs. instructors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust level of detail, notation, and motivation; explicitly state assumptions about prerequisite knowledge and use examples appropriate to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriately cite and attribute sources, prior results, and literature used in mathematical exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess for proper citations, clarity about which results are original vs. quoted, and correct use of bibliographic conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using visuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use diagrams, figures, and other visual aids to clarify concepts, examples, or proof ideas where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate clarity, labeling, captioning, and whether visuals genuinely aid understanding rather than distract; see linked handouts for best practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wording and punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ clear prose, correct grammar, and punctuation to make mathematical text readable and unambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess clarity of sentences, avoidance of ambiguous phrasing, and correct use of punctuation to disambiguate formulas and clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose consistent, unambiguous notation and introduce notation clearly when first used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should check for overloaded symbols, unclear indices, and whether notation choices help or hinder comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: LaTeX and typesetting (including labels on figures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use appropriate typesetting tools (LaTeX, LyX) and good figure labeling practices to produce readable mathematical documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate presentation quality: readable equations, consistent formatting, legible figures, and correct figure/table labels and references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider informal math communication (discussion, collaborative explanation) as a venue with different norms than formal writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of informal work should focus on clarity of ideas conveyed, productive dialogue, and contribution to group understanding rather than formal polish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentations: engaging the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: For oral presentations, engage listeners through clear delivery, appropriate pacing, eye contact, and interactive elements when suitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use practice presentations and peer feedback; evaluate delivery, clarity of exposition, use of visuals, and responsiveness to audience cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice presentations and peer critique for presentations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use rehearsal and structured peer critique to improve presentation quality and provide formative assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment instruments (e.g., Presentation Evaluation Form) and guided peer feedback protocols are recommended to give concrete, actionable feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer critique on writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use structured peer review as a formative assessment method for student writing, with clear criteria and comment codes if desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide rubrics or comment codes to guide peers; use peer feedback for revision cycles and instructor moderation to ensure quality of comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing to learn: using writing to help students learn math
rubrics_metrics.description: Use writing assignments not only to assess communication but also as a tool to deepen students' conceptual understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments that ask students to explain thinking, reflect on problem-solving, or teach a concept can serve dual formative and summative roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative writing and presentations
rubrics_metrics.description: Address writing and speaking that involve quantitative data, calculations, or statistical claims; clarity and correct interpretation are essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess precision in numerical statements, proper representation of uncertainty, and correct use of tables/graphs in support of arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for professional-level mathematical communication, including appropriate tone, conventions, and expectations for publication or conference presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether work conforms to disciplinary norms for professionalism, audience, and venue; include proofreading, citation norms, and ethical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feedback and assessment for writing (grading and providing feedback on writing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical approaches to grading student writing: rubrics, comment strategies, formative feedback cycles, and constructive critique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See the site's linked handouts on grading writing for specific rubrics, sample comments, and strategies for timely, actionable feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feedback and assessment for presentations (grading and providing feedback on presentations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical approaches to evaluating oral presentations, including rubrics, timing of feedback, and balancing content vs. delivery in scoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use structured forms (e.g., Presentation Evaluation Form) and combine instructor, peer, and self-assessment for comprehensive feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric resources and templates (e.g., Rubric for term paper drafts, Final paper evaluation grid, Presentation Evaluation Form, Rubric for short writing, Comments codes for mathematics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete rubric templates and comment-code lists provided as downloadable resources to assess specific genres (term papers, short writing, presentations, problem submissions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these ready-made grids and comment codes as starting points; adapt to course goals and share rubrics with students before assignment submission to align expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structuring and grading seminars
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on how to design seminar assessments and choose grade distributions for seminar courses that include communication components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider frequency of presentations, participation grading, and integration of written components; see linked page for choices and trade-offs when assigning grades.
